Google dropped A2A, an open protocol for AI agents to talk to each other. Microsoft says every worker will soon be an “agent boss” managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. Visa and Mastercard are preparing for AI shopping agents. Meanwhile, CIOs are asking: Is this real or just hype?

This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the rapidly evolving AI agent landscape. Major tech firms unveiled competing visions for how autonomous AI will transform enterprise work, protocol wars emerged, and security partnerships formed to address enterprise concerns.

The Protocol Wars Begin

The most significant technical development of April was Google’s launch of A2A (Agent-to-Agent), an open protocol designed to enable AI agents to communicate directly with each other. Announced on April 9 , A2A addresses a fundamental bottleneck in multi-agent systems: interoperability.

The protocol allows AI agents from different developers and platforms to exchange information and coordinate actions without requiring custom integrations for each pair of systems. This is the foundational infrastructure needed for multi-agent workflows to scale beyond single-vendor ecosystems. As The Stack reported , Google’s announcement immediately sparked a “protocol war” with competing standards.

The competitive landscape includes:

  • A2A (Agent-to-Agent): Google’s open protocol for universal agent communication
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): Anthropic’s protocol for connecting AI models to external data sources
  • ACP (Agent Communication Protocol): An alternative approach from other vendors

The emergence of multiple competing standards reflects the high stakes. The protocol that achieves broad adoption will shape how agents interact for years to come. Vendors are positioning their protocols as the foundation for enterprise agent ecosystems.

Google complemented the A2A announcement with new agent building tools and an open source framework added to Vertex AI for building agents. These tools give developers practical ways to implement A2A in their applications.

Enterprise interest in agent interoperability is real. TCS partnered with Google Cloud on A2A interoperability to help enterprises build “future-ready” agent systems. The partnership signals that large systems integrators are already preparing to implement agent-to-agent communication for their clients.

The protocol question remains unresolved. Which standard will win? The answer may come down to which vendor can attract the most developer adoption and enterprise partnerships. Google’s first-mover advantage with A2A is significant, but Anthropic’s MCP has gained traction through its integration with popular AI models. The next few months will be critical in determining which protocol becomes the de facto standard for agent communication.

Microsoft’s Agent Boss Future

Microsoft made its clearest statement yet on AI agents in April: every human worker will soon be an “agent boss” , managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. This isn’t framed as incremental productivity improvement—it’s presented as an org chart transformation.

The vision comes from Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index, which highlights how AI agents are reshaping the future of work . Microsoft envisions a workplace where each employee manages a team of AI agents, with human-to-agent ratios becoming a critical metric for organizational success. As Constellation Research reported , these ratios “will be critical to success as new roles emerge.”

The practical implementation involves several new capabilities:

Azure AI Foundry received new capabilities for building advanced agentic applications . The platform now provides unified tooling for developing, deploying, and managing AI agents at enterprise scale. These enhancements aim to simplify the journey from prototype to production for agentic systems.

Agent flows were introduced as a new concept for transforming automation with AI-first workflows . Agent flows provide a visual way to design multi-step workflows where AI agents coordinate with each other and with humans to complete complex tasks.

The Copilot Control System was announced to bring “order and management” to potential AI agent sprawl. As enterprises deploy dozens or hundreds of agents, managing them becomes a challenge—similar to the API sprawl problem of previous decades. The control system provides centralized governance.

Microsoft also announced three new AI agents for autonomous contact centers , targeting customer service as a key use case. These agents can handle routine inquiries, route complex issues to humans, and learn from interactions over time.

Customer deployments show the vision in practice. NTT DATA is transforming its enterprise with agentic AI in Microsoft Fabric and Azure AI Foundry. Roland Berger relies on AI agents and Microsoft Azure to create “more time for value creation.”

Microsoft’s broader messaging frames agentic AI as driving AI-first business transformation . The company’s research division also published on how human-agent teams will reshape the workforce .

Not everyone accepts the “agent boss” framing uncritically. As CIO.com explored , Microsoft sees AI agents shaking up org charts and eliminating traditional functions—but The Guardian noted the uncertainty around what this means for workers. Geekwire characterized the shift as Microsoft seeing “humans as ‘agent bosses,’ upending the workplace.”

Additional Microsoft announcements included new computer use capabilities in Copilot Studio for UI automation, guidance on identifying readiness for AI-first development , and a report on agents of change unlocking potential .

Microsoft also tapped AI agents and partners to scale and automate cybersecurity protections, extending the agentic vision into security operations.

The Great Platform Rush

Google wasn’t the only company building agent infrastructure in April. A wave of platform announcements from major vendors revealed a land grab for developer mindshare.

Google’s Double Play

Beyond the A2A protocol, Google announced the Agent Development Kit , which lets enterprises “rapidly prototype and deploy AI agents without recoding.” The kit provides pre-built components and templates to accelerate agent development.

Google Cloud also unveiled an AI Agent Marketplace at its Next conference, creating a centralized location for discovering and deploying pre-built agents. The marketplace approach mirrors the app store model, aiming to create an ecosystem around Google’s agent platform.

Nvidia Goes GA

Nvidia announced the general availability of NeMo tools for building AI agents . The NeMo Microservices are designed to create an “AI agent data flywheel”—as agents interact with systems, they generate data that can improve future agent performance.

Nvidia also unveiled the AI-Q Blueprint for transforming AI agent systems into digital workforces, and published technical content on building enterprise AI agents with advanced open Llama Nemotron reasoning models.

Enterprise Governance

Dataiku introduced AI Agents to unify and govern enterprise agent deployments . The focus on governance reflects enterprise concerns about managing agent sprawl, ensuring compliance, and maintaining oversight as agents proliferate.

**Futurum Group analyzed Oracle’s AI Agent Studio](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/is-oracles-ai-agent-studio-the-missing-layer-for-enterprise-wide-automation/) , positioning it as “the missing layer for enterprise-wide automation.” Oracle’s approach emphasizes unified management and integration with existing enterprise systems.

Other Platform Announcements

  • Writer unveiled “AI HQ” as a platform betting on agents to transform enterprise work
  • Amazon Web Services published on building multi-agent systems with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock
  • Camunda added AI agents to its process orchestration platform

Security: Agents as Threat and Shield

AI agents are reshaping cybersecurity in two directions—agents are being deployed to defend against threats, but they’re also creating new attack vectors.

Defensive Agents

Security vendors are rapidly incorporating agents into their products:

Vectra AI completed its groundbreaking agent portfolio , positioning its agentic AI systems as “setting new standard” for threat detection and security team efficiency.

Abnormal AI launched breakthrough AI agents to reimagine security awareness training and provide instant board-ready data insights. The agents aim to automate security training while providing executives with visibility into security posture.

Jit launched AI agents to ease AppSec workload , bringing automation to application security testing.

Nvidia published on advancing cybersecurity operations with agentic AI systems and how agentic AI enables the next leap in cybersecurity .

Google, Radiant, and Qevlar expanded AI agent use for SOCs (security operations centers).

Solutions Review catalogued the top AI agents for cybersecurity teams .

Securing the Agents

As agents become more powerful, securing them becomes critical:

CyberArk and Accenture partnered to secure enterprise AI agents . The partnership combines CyberArk’s identity security with Accenture’s AI Refinery to address what CyberArk calls identity security for AI agents .

Sentra introduced Data Security for AI Agents as a solution to secure the next generation of business automation .

TechTarget explored how AI agents raise stakes in identity and access management .

CIO Dive reported that IT leaders want better security and data privacy from AI agents.

New Attack Vectors

MIT Technology Review warned that cyberattacks by AI agents are coming . The article explores how autonomous AI could be used to conduct more sophisticated, adaptive cyberattacks at scale.

CFO Dive noted that AI agents emerge as potential targets for cyberattackers—a new threat vector where attackers compromise agents themselves to gain access to enterprise systems.

Company Security Focus Approach
CyberArk + Accenture Identity Security Partnership
Vectra AI Threat Detection AI-Powered Agents
Abnormal AI Security Training Awareness Agents
Sentra Data Security Agent Protection
Jit AppSec Workload Automation

Shopping With AI Agents

E-commerce is quietly becoming the first major battleground for practical AI agent applications.

Amazon’s new AI agent will shop third-party sites for you . The agent browses external websites to find products, compare prices, and make purchases—extending Amazon’s reach beyond its own marketplace.

Mastercard’s Agent Pay transforms how enterprises use AI search by eliminating window switching. The product enables AI agents to complete purchases directly within enterprise workflows, removing friction between search and transaction.

Visa gives AI shopping agents “intelligent commerce ” capabilities by extending its payment rails to support agent-initiated transactions. AP News reported that Visa “wants to give artificial intelligence ‘agents’ your credit card.”

Visa CMO Frank Cooper III discussed the company’s bet on AI agents in an interview about “culture, commerce and marketing’s next frontier.”

Nvidia explored how AI agents enhance online shopping , outlining use cases for personalized recommendations, automated comparison shopping, and conversational commerce.

These developments point to a future where AI agents become primary participants in e-commerce—representing consumers in transactions, negotiating prices, and making purchasing decisions. The payment networks’ early positioning suggests they see agents as both an opportunity and a threat to existing commerce models.

Healthcare’s Agent Experiment

Healthcare emerged in April as a key early adopter of AI agent technology, with several focused deployments in high-value use cases.

Infinitus launched the first trusted voice AI agents for healthcare , targeting administrative workflows like prior authorization and benefits verification.

Cedar rolled out an AI voice agent to tackle patients’ medical billing questions , addressing a major pain point in healthcare finance.

Seattle Children’s teamed up with Google Cloud to develop a decision-support AI agent for healthcare providers. The clinical decision support agent aims to help clinicians access relevant information more quickly.

Google Cloud sees multi-agent AI systems as healthcare’s “next frontier” , expanding AI agent tools for healthcare .

Oracle reported that AI agents show promise in transforming healthcare .

PwC explored how Google Cloud and AI agents transform healthcare .

Relatient launched Dash Voice AI Agent to automate patient appointment management in call centers .

eHealth introduced AI voice agents to enhance customer experience in health plan selection .

Healthcare’s adoption pattern is notable: providers are focusing agents on administrative tasks (billing, appointments, prior authorization) rather than clinical decision-making. This reflects both regulatory caution and practical opportunity—healthcare has significant administrative overhead that agents can address without requiring clinical validation.

Workforce: Hype vs Reality

The hype machine surrounding AI agents reached new levels in April, even as enterprises struggled with basic questions about what AI agents actually are and how to deploy them.

The Reality Check

ZDNet reported that 60% of AI agents work in IT departments . The finding suggests that despite the hype about agents transforming every business function, actual deployment is heavily concentrated in technical functions.

CIO.com explored how CIOs struggle with the definition of what makes a true AI agent. The terminology confusion—chatbots vs. copilots vs. agents vs. agentic AI—creates challenges for procurement and evaluation.

SiliconANGLE examined the long road to agentic AI , contrasting hype with enterprise reality.

HR Executive asked whether AI agent implementation has stalled and whether HR can propel it forward.

Actuia considered whether 2025 is the year of maturity for enterprise AI agents.

Cutting Through the Hype

Salesforce introduced a 5-level framework for AI agents that cuts through the hype . The framework provides maturity levels to help enterprises distinguish between basic automation and true agentic systems.

UiPath AI agents blend with RPA amid industry hype and doubts , suggesting a more incremental evolution than revolutionary change.

Digiday profiled Salesforce’s transformation from CRM giant to “digital labor” provider , exploring how the company aims to “stand above the hype” with agentic AI.

Cautionary Tales

A company apologized after its AI support agent invented a policy that caused user uproar. The incident highlights the risks of autonomous agents making statements or commitments beyond their authority—a governance challenge that enterprises must address.

Professors staffed a fake company entirely with AI agents in an experiment covered by Futurism and DIGIT . The results were mixed, showing both promise and limitation in current agent capabilities.

Who’s Interested?

ZDNet analyzed the 4 types of people interested in AI agents and what businesses can learn from them.

Socradar asked whether AI agents are hype or reality .

NetworkWorld explored the distinction between AI agents vs. agentic AI and what enterprises actually want.

Market Signals: Funding and Startups

Venture capital activity and startup moves provide signals about where the market is placing bets:

  • Artisan raises $25M with a provocative “stop hiring humans” pitch —though the startup is still hiring humans itself
  • a16z backs UK startup Dex to scale an “AI talent agent” and recruitment matchmaker
  • Model ML seeks to acquire AI agent companies according to its CEO
  • A new agency is staffed with more AI agents than people and wants to keep it that way , according to Ad Age
  • Make launched Make AI Agents to add real-time intelligence to no-code automation

The funding pattern suggests investors are targeting specific horizontal use cases (recruitment, automation) rather than general-purpose agent platforms. The “stop hiring humans” framing generates attention, but the reality is more nuanced—companies are hiring humans to build and manage agents.

Developer Experience: Agents That Code

Software development remains a key use case for AI agents:

  • Augment Code launched Augment Agent as an AI pair programmer that deeply understands codebases and learns as you work
  • Microsoft Research published on Debug-gym exploring whether AI agents can lighten developers’ debugging load
  • DevOps.com explored how AI agents are reshaping the developer experience
  • Anthropic shared best practices for Claude Code agentic coding
  • Augment Code published how to prompt your agent with 8 tips and best practices for using AI coding agents

Coding agents benefit from clear evaluation criteria (does the code work?) and continuous feedback loops from integrated development environments. This makes them one of the more mature agent categories.

Industry Snapshot

AI agents are spreading across industries:

  • Adobe is building AI agents for Photoshop and Premiere Pro , including an agent that can show you how to use Photoshop
  • OneTrack launched AiOn as the first AI agent platform for autonomous logistics operations
  • MineOS unveiled an AI agent to transform data privacy management
  • SK Telecom touted AI agent ‘Aster’ as the future of telecom innovation
  • Atlassian shared customer impressions of putting the Rovo AI agent to work
  • Baidu rolled out new AI agent Xinxiang for Android
  • KPMG reported that most companies are just test-driving AI agents
  • Microsoft explored how AI and intelligent agents are transforming local government
  • Real estate and travel industries explored agents for homebuyers and vacation planning
  • Counterpoint Research analyzed how smartphone OEMs can stay competitive in the era of AI agents
  • Computer Weekly explored how AI agents will reshape telecoms

Looking Ahead: What April Means for Agents

April 2025 was a foundational month for AI agents. The developments weren’t incremental—they were structural changes to how agents will be built, deployed, and managed in enterprises.

The protocol wars (A2A vs MCP vs ACP) will determine how agents interoperate. No standard has won yet, and fragmentation is likely to persist in the near term. Enterprises should prepare for multi-protocol environments.

The “agent boss” vision from Microsoft represents one possible future for work—humans managing teams of AI agents. But other vendors envision different models (human-AI collaboration, agents as assistants rather than subordinates). The org chart of the future is still being negotiated.

Security partnerships like CyberArk + Accenture address what could be a blocking issue for enterprise adoption. If agents can’t be secured, they won’t be deployed. The emergence of specialized agent security offerings suggests the market is taking this seriously.

Healthcare and commerce are leading use cases with clear ROI and relatively lower regulatory barriers. These industries provide a preview of how agents will transform workflows in other sectors.

The hype is real, but so are the challenges. CIOs struggle with definitions. Implementation has stalled in some places. Early failures like the policy-inventing agent show the risks. According to ZDnet, 60% of AI agents work in IT departments—suggesting transformation is concentrated, not universal.

The market is moving from “what are agents?” to “which platform and protocol win?” Expect the protocol war to intensify, security offerings to multiply, and enterprises to run more pilots. The next six months will determine whether 2025 is the year agents mature—or another hype cycle peak.

This comprehensive review covers 118 articles published in February 2025, surveying the rapid emergence of AI agents as autonomous digital workers. OpenAI launched Operator, an AI agent that autonomously browses the web and completes tasks. Google unveiled an AI co-scientist for research. Meanwhile, Workday, ServiceNow, and SAP are racing to build infrastructure to manage fleets of AI agents as digital employees.

The Big Launches

OpenAI and Google led February’s product announcements, introducing AI agents that autonomously navigate the web and conduct research.

OpenAI launched Operator, an AI agent that browses the web and completes tasks on behalf of users. Unlike traditional chatbots, Operator autonomously navigates websites, fills out forms, and clicks buttons. The agent rolled out to ChatGPT Pro users in multiple countries in February, available for most Pro users at the $200/month tier. Operator uses a computer-vision model to “see” web pages and take action.

OpenAI also announced Deep Research, an AI agent powered by the o3 model that conducts multi-step research tasks. The agent achieves a 26.6% accuracy on “Humanity’s Last Exam” benchmark across 3,000 questions and 100 subjects. Deep Research browses the web for 5 to 30 minutes, synthesizing information from hundreds of sources into comprehensive reports with citations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described it as “like a superpower; experts on demand!” The capability launched first for Pro users with 100 queries per month , with expansion planned to Plus, Team, and Enterprise tiers.

Google introduced an AI co-scientist, a multi-agent system built with Gemini 2.0 designed to help scientists generate novel hypotheses and research proposals. The system uses specialized agents—Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review—that mirror the scientific method. In biomedical applications, the AI co-scientist proposed three novel drug repurposing candidates for acute myeloid leukemia that were validated in laboratory experiments. The company is opening access through a Trusted Tester Program for research organizations.

Google also launched “Ask for Me,” an experimental AI agent that calls businesses on a user’s behalf. Currently available through Search Labs in the U.S., the agent calls mechanics and nail salons to inquire about pricing and availability. This represents a potential evolution of Google’s discontinued Duplex technology and signals a move toward machine-to-machine customer service interactions. Gartner predicts that 20% of contact center traffic could come from machine customers by 2026.

The browser-use agent space is seeing competition. Convergence’s Proxy agent scored 88% on the WebVoyager benchmark , compared to Operator’s 87%. Proxy offers an unlimited plan at $20/month versus Operator’s $200/month Pro tier, though OpenAI’s agent benefits from integration with the broader ChatGPT ecosystem.

Enterprise Platform Wars

The most significant trend in February was the race to build AI agent management infrastructure. Workday, ServiceNow, and SAP are positioning themselves as the systems of record for managing AI agents as digital employees.

Workday unveiled the Workday Agent System of Record, a platform to help organizations manage their entire fleet of AI agents. The system provides tools for governance, management, and optimization of digital workforces, including onboarding, role definition, cost tracking, and compliance. Workday processes over 800 billion transactions annually through its Illuminate AI platform, giving it deep visibility into workforce operations.

Workday also introduced role-based AI agents with configurable skills that can perform hundreds of individual tasks. New agents announced include contract, payroll, financial auditing, and policy agents. The approach treats AI agents like employees in an HR system—a shift from “using AI” to “managing a workforce of AI agents.” Workday serves as the system of record for 10,500 companies worldwide.

“The workforce of the future will include both humans and AI agents,” said Aneel Bhusri , Workday’s co-founder and executive chair. “Businesses that don’t learn to manage this incredibly complex reality will fall quickly behind.”

SAP unleashed several “ready-to-use” AI agents powered by its Joule virtual assistant. The agents are available across customer service, sales, and finance, including a Cash Collection agent that collaborates across departments to resolve disputes. SAP also introduced a custom agent builder in Joule Studio, allowing citizen developers to create tailored AI agents using a no-code tool. The company is positioning Joule as an “AI orchestrator” that can assemble teams of agents to perform complex end-to-end processes.

ServiceNow is positioning itself as the “control tower” for AI agents across IT, customer service, and HR workflows. Its AI Agent Orchestrator and AI Agent Studio enable organizations to build and manage agents with real-time access to enterprise data through the Workflow Data Fabric. The focus is on cross-functional enterprise automation, particularly in IT service management.

Oracle announced AI agents for HR through its Fusion Cloud HCM suite. The agents help HR leaders reshape the employee experience by automating routine tasks and providing intelligent recommendations. Oracle also expanded its B2C Service Center with Agent Suggestions powered by generative AI, allowing live agents to receive contextually relevant suggestions from multiple data sources including OCI Generative AI, Azure OpenAI, and custom REST endpoints.

The competition is intense. Salesforce, which announced Agentforce 2.0 in December 2024, issued a revenue forecast that fell short of analyst expectations, with projected revenue of $40.5 billion to $40.9 billion for fiscal year 2026 versus the $41.5 billion estimate. This tempered enthusiasm about AI agent returns, with CFO Dive reporting that Salesforce expects “modest” returns from its AI agent push this year.

Company Rollouts

Enterprises are deploying AI agents across diverse sectors, with concrete results emerging in healthcare, financial services, customer service, and logistics.

Healthcare

Innovaccer launched a suite of AI agents called “Agents of Care” designed to automate repetitive administrative tasks that contribute to clinician burnout. The agents handle scheduling, patient intake, referrals, and 24-hour support for patient inquiries. One agent conducts voice-activated protocol intake calls, asking patients questions about their emergency room visit and scheduling follow-ups. A referral agent connects patients with specialists and manages appointment logistics.

The rollout comes amid a projected shortage of 100,000 healthcare workers by 2028, according to consulting firm Mercer. Clinicians spend nearly nine hours per week on documentation alone, according to a Google Cloud study. Innovaccer, which recently raised $275 million in funding from investors including Generation Investment Management and Microsoft’s M12, is testing the agents at five health systems with general availability planned in two to three months.

Financial Services

BNY Mellon is managing “armies of AI agents” through its Eliza tool, an open-source system that enables multi-agent negotiations. The bank, America’s oldest, has deployed AI agents that can negotiate with each other to optimize internal processes. The system began development in 2023 and was released in 2024, with plans to upgrade to Eliza 2.0.

Goldman Sachs and Capital One are preparing for self-driving AI agents, according to American Banker. The financial institutions are exploring how agents can automate workflows while maintaining compliance in highly regulated environments. Routable added a fraud-detecting AI agent to its AP automation platform, identifying suspicious invoices and payment anomalies.

Customer Service

Cresta announced rapidly scaling AI voice agents in production, with strong results from deployments at Brinks Home Security. The AI Agent combines cutting-edge language models with business logic to deliver empathetic, human-like conversations that resolve complex issues. Brinks Home reported a 30-point increase in Net Promoter Score following the deployment.

Jotform launched AI Agents to transform customer service with a no-code solution. The platform enables organizations to deploy AI-powered virtual agents that manage inquiries and guide users through complex processes like booking, onboarding, and appointment scheduling. Jotform has over 30 million users worldwide .

HubSpot’s Agent.ai platform raced past 500,000 users after launching at INBOUND 2024. The platform, founded by HubSpot CTO Dharmesh Shah, grew from 250,000 users at the start of 2025, demonstrating rapid adoption. More than 5,000 people have used the low-code tool to build custom agents, and users have submitted 13,000 ratings and reviews with an average of 3.99 stars.

Real Estate

Christie’s is using AI agents to sell real estate and has generated $100 million in sales through the technology, according to Fox Business. The real estate giant’s Porta da Frente division has deployed agents to handle property transactions, demonstrating concrete ROI from AI agent adoption.

Telecom and Logistics

Deutsche Telekom partnered with Google Cloud on agentic AI for autonomous networks. The collaboration aims to develop AI agents that can manage network operations autonomously, improving efficiency and reducing manual intervention.

FourKites unveiled Tracy & Sam, two AI agents for supply chain efficiency. Tracy handles track and trace functions, automating repetitive tasks 24/7 and proactively contacting carriers to ensure data accuracy. Sam focuses on supplier collaboration, processing purchase orders and invoices. Early adopter Unilever reported improvements within four weeks of implementing Tracy, with the agent helping exception management and tracking quality. FourKites claims the Digital Workforce can increase shipment handling by 40% and automate up to 80% of routine tasks.

Sector Company Use Case Status
Healthcare Innovaccer Scheduling, patient intake, referrals Launched, testing at 5 systems
Financial Services BNY Mellon Managing agent fleets, multi-agent negotiations In production
Real Estate Christie’s Property sales $100M in sales
Customer Service Cresta Voice agents with Brinks Home Scaling in production
Customer Service HubSpot/Agent.ai Network of autonomous agents 500,000+ users
Telecom Deutsche Telekom Network operations with Google Cloud Pilot
Logistics FourKites Tracy & Sam efficiency agents Launched

Developer Tools & Infrastructure

A new distribution model is emerging: AI agent marketplaces. Cloud platforms are also making it easier to build agents, and developer tools are adding agent capabilities.

Marketplaces & Stores

Olas launched the first-ever AI agent store with $13.8 million in backing. The decentralized marketplace enables developers to publish and monetize AI agents, similar to app stores. The funding raised by Olas aims to accelerate the development of an ecosystem where agents can be discovered, composed, and deployed.

Enso launched an AI agent marketplace in partnership with LangChain. The platform offers pre-built agents for business tasks, enabling organizations to deploy AI automation without building from scratch.

Cloud Platforms

Microsoft Azure announced Azure AI Agent Service in public preview, available through AI Foundry SDK and Portal. The service enables developers to build secure, stateful, autonomous AI agents in code-first environments. Microsoft also unveiled GPT-4.5, the latest general-purpose model, alongside specialized models including Phi-4, Phi-4-Vision, Phi-4-Coding, and Phi-4-Audio. The Azure AI Foundry model library now exceeds 1,800 offerings .

Amazon Web Services (AWS) introduced Amazon Q Developer Agents, streamlining development with AI-powered coding assistance. AWS also published guidance on building agentic AI solutions with DeepSeek-R1, CrewAI, and Amazon SageMaker AI.

Google Cloud announced tools to build scalable AI agents with Langbase and the Gemini API. The platform enables developers to create agents that leverage Gemini 2.0 for complex reasoning tasks.

Snowflake launched AI agents powered by Anthropic’s Claude, integrating the large language model into its data cloud platform. The agents can analyze data and generate insights within Snowflake’s infrastructure.

Zoho Corporation announced Zia Agents, a platform supporting autonomous agents across its portfolio of 100+ products. Zia Agents, Agent Studio, and Agent Marketplace empower enterprises to access, build, and distribute intelligent digital agents. The company, which onboarded 110,000 new customers in 2024, is previewing pre-built, task-specific agents that will deploy across its combined portfolio.

Developer Tools

GitHub Copilot unveiled “The agent awakens,” adding agent capabilities to the development platform. The upgrade enables Copilot to handle more complex coding workflows autonomously.

Postman introduced AI Agent Builder with three key features: visual agent design, testing, and deployment. The tool helps developers create agents that interact with APIs.

Docker added agent capabilities for containerized applications, enabling AI-driven operations within its platform.

Infrastructure Considerations

The infrastructure stack for AI agents is evolving. The New Stack reported on why AI agents need an operational database , highlighting the need for databases that can handle the state management, transaction consistency, and real-time requirements of agentic workloads.

Cisco’s Outshift group predicted that average-size organizations will deploy 20,000 AI agents , with enterprises handling hundreds of thousands. This has sparked discussion of an “Internet of Agents”—an open, interoperable framework for agent-to-agent communication.

Research and Innovation

Research institutions and companies are exploring novel applications of AI agents, from robotics to chip design.

Microsoft Research introduced Magma, an AI foundation model that combines visual and language processing to control both software interfaces and robotic systems. Unlike prior systems requiring separate models for perception and control, Magma integrates these abilities. The model scored 80.0 on the VQAv2 benchmark , higher than GPT-4V’s 77.2, and achieved 87.4 on the POPE benchmark. Microsoft plans to release the code publicly on GitHub.

NVIDIA introduced Marco, a multi-AI agent framework for chip design. The configurable graph-based system enables multiple agents to collaborate on complex chip design tasks, representing a novel application of agentic AI in semiconductor engineering.

University of Oulu researchers developed MAI (metacognitive AI agent), an AI tutor that taught physics to 12-13-year-old students in Finland. Unlike traditional AI applications that provide ready-made answers, MAI supports independent problem-solving by prompting students to think. The pilot found that students “appreciated MAI’s prompting feature” and that the agent helped group work dynamics.

Napkin AI launched a ‘design agency’ of AI agents that generates professional graphics from text prompts in under five seconds. The company doubled its user base to 2 million in six weeks. The platform uses a team of specialized AI agents—an orchestrator LLM assigns tasks to styling, rendering, and layout agents—demonstrating a vertical approach to agentic AI.

Logie AI launched “Influencer’s Agent Army” for affiliate marketing, automating influencer campaign management at scale.

Various researchers are exploring car-buying agents, AI agents that would handle vehicle research, pricing negotiation, and purchase. Computerworld reported on how an AI agent could help you buy your next car .

Microsoft published ExACT (Improving AI agents’ decision-making via test-time compute scaling), a research framework for enhancing agent performance through increased computational investment during task execution.

Challenges and Concerns

While AI agents are advancing rapidly, researchers and practitioners are raising important concerns about deployment, safety, and societal impact.

Researchers warned that fully autonomous AI agents “should not be deployed.” A paper reviewed in Process Excellence Network stated, “We find no clear benefit of fully autonomous AI agents, but many foreseeable harms from ceding full human control.” The researchers found that risks increase with system autonomy, particularly safety risks that affect human life. They recommended adoption of agent levels, human control mechanisms, and safety verification.

A Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University study found that some workers risk becoming overly reliant on generative AI, with problem-solving skills declining as a result. The survey of 319 knowledge workers collected 936 examples of AI use, finding that higher confidence in AI correlates with less critical thinking.

Job displacement concerns are emerging. Microsoft executive Georg Glantschnig told CFO Dive that some finance jobs may “disappear” as AI agents automate labor-intensive processes like financial close. However, he noted that new roles like “agent business administrators” are emerging.

Security risks are multiplying. Malwarebytes reported on new AI agents that could hold people for ransom, representing an evolution of ransomware threats.

Business model questions persist. Reuters Breakingviews analysis noted that AI agents have a clear mission but hazy business models. Investors see vast potential—Ark Investments estimates AI agents could enable $9 trillion of global e-commerce sales by 2030—but monetization paths remain uncertain.

Confusion about what agents actually are persists. UC Today documented “AI Agent Confusion” , noting that the term ranges from simple chatbots to fully autonomous systems, making it difficult for enterprises to evaluate solutions.

UX concerns are growing. Built In identified three things needed before AI agents go mainstream: improved trust and transparency, better error handling, and seamless integration into existing workflows.

Privacy issues are emerging. SC Media outlined five privacy concerns around agentic AI, including data collection, surveillance, and the potential for agents to expose sensitive information.

Responsible AI is becoming a priority. IBM published “The Rise of Responsible AI Agents” , emphasizing the need for ethical development practices.

Legal perspectives are emerging. Above the Law published guidance for in-house counsel on agents versus agentic AI, highlighting legal considerations for enterprise adoption.

Implementation challenges are significant. A Constellation Research report noted that AI agents bring new consumption models to SaaS, asking whether this represents a “Goldilocks or headache” for enterprises managing software costs.

Funding and Startups

Startup activity and funding rounds reflect growing investor interest in AI agent infrastructure and applications.

Olas raised $13.8 million to launch its decentralized AI agent store, according to VentureBeat . The funding aims to build a marketplace where agents can be discovered, composed, and deployed.

Qeen.ai, an AI agents for e-commerce startup founded by Google and DeepMind alumni, raised a $10 million seed round . The company, which employs 50 people, offers autonomous agents for e-commerce automation.

Pinkfish emerged from stealth with a $7.6 million pre-seed round led by Norwest Venture Partners. The startup helps enterprises build AI agents through natural language processing, with more than 200 integrations including Salesforce and Zendesk. Customers include Ipsy, Elevate, and Talkdesk.

SoftBank and OpenAI partnered to push AGI and agents, according to Axios . The partnership aims to accelerate the development of artificial general intelligence with Japanese focus.

Nvidia’s revenue is surging from agentic AI demand. CEO Jensen Huang reported that Blackwell GPU architecture booked $11 billion in Q4 revenue, with data center revenues more than doubling. The company sees agentic AI as the next stage after generative AI, with “physical AI” like robots following after.

India accounts for 40% of AI agent deployments globally for Automation Anywhere, driven by global capability centers and large enterprises. The company reported two-fold growth in AI agent deals and an 80% success rate from proof-of-concept to production.

Looking Ahead

Three distinct trends emerge from February’s developments:

First, AI agents are moving from prototypes to production. OpenAI’s Operator and Google’s AI co-scientist represent productized agents available to users, not just research demonstrations. The focus is shifting from “what can agents do?” to “how do we deploy and manage them at scale?”

Second, enterprises are building agent management systems. Workday’s Agent System of Record, ServiceNow’s AI Agent Orchestrator, and SAP’s Joule represent infrastructure for treating AI agents as digital employees. This reflects the recognition that managing fleets of agents requires new categories of enterprise software.

Third, new distribution channels are emerging. Agent marketplaces from Olas and Enso represent a new model for discovering and deploying AI agents. This could accelerate adoption by making agents easier to find and integrate.

The corporate venturing community is actively investing. Global Corporate Venturing reported that companies are rushing to invest in AI agent startups, sensing both opportunity and competitive threat.

Looking at a 10-year horizon, NFX predicted the rise of an “AI agent economy” , where agent marketplaces become the primary distribution channel for software and services.

However, expectations are outpacing reality. IBM’s analysis of “AI Agents in 2025: Expectations vs. Reality” noted that while excitement is high, many deployments remain in pilot or experimentation phases. Salesforce’s tempered revenue forecast reinforces that AI agent adoption will be gradual rather than explosive.

The workplace of the future will include both humans and AI agents. As Axios noted , workplace chat will feature more AI agents and fewer humans over time. The question is not whether AI agents will enter the workforce, but how quickly enterprises will adapt their management practices, security protocols, and workforce strategies to accommodate them.

2025 is shaping up to be the year of enterprise experimentation with AI agents—testing use cases, building management infrastructure, and learning what works. The transition to widespread production deployments will take longer, but the foundation is being laid now.

OpenAI released Operator, a research preview of an AI agent that browses the web and performs tasks autonomously. The launch signals a shift from chatbots to agents, with enterprises racing to adopt agentic AI while researchers tackle reliability and safety challenges.

This comprehensive review covers 118 articles published between January and February 2025, surveying the rapid evolution of AI agents from research curiosities to enterprise products.

The Lead: OpenAI’s Operator Enters the Arena

OpenAI has released Operator, a research preview of an AI agent that uses the Computer-Using Agent (CUA) model to control a browser through a visual interface. Rather than relying on website APIs, Operator interacts with web pages the way a human does—by clicking buttons, typing in forms, and navigating menus—allowing it to perform tasks like booking travel, ordering groceries, and filling out forms.

The performance benchmarks are notable but reveal the limitations of current technology. Operator achieves an 87% success rate on the WebVoyager benchmark, which measures real website navigation capabilities. On WebArena, which tests ecommerce and content management scenarios, it reaches 58.1%. However, on the OSWorld benchmark for general computer tasks, Operator scores 38.1% compared to 72.4% for human performance, highlighting the gap remaining before agents match human reliability across diverse tasks.

Operator is available initially to ChatGPT Pro subscribers at $200 per month, with OpenAI planning to expand availability to other tiers later. The research preview is limited to the United States and not available in Europe at launch due to regulatory considerations.

OpenAI has partnered with major platforms for testing, including eBay , Instacart , and DoorDash , to explore how the agent can handle real-world tasks like grocery shopping and food delivery.

Early reviews indicate that Operator still requires significant supervision. Bloomberg’s testing found the agent needs “adult supervision” for complex tasks, particularly when unexpected situations arise. The research preview designation acknowledges these limitations—this is an early look at agentic capabilities, not a finished product ready for unsupervised operation.

Operator’s launch is part of a broader industry trend. Google announced Project Mariner in December 2024, and Anthropic introduced “Computer Use” in October 2024. What sets OpenAI’s entry apart is the scale of its distribution through the existing ChatGPT user base and the company’s positioning of 2025 as “the year of agentic AI.”

Platform Wars: The Agent Builder Eruption

Operator isn’t alone in the market. A wave of platform announcements from enterprise giants demonstrates how agentic AI has become a competitive battleground across the software industry.

Enterprise Platforms

ServiceNow delivered what may be the most comprehensive enterprise agent announcement of the period. The company introduced thousands of pre-configured AI agents , a no-code AI Agent Studio for building custom agents, and an AI Agent Orchestrator for managing multi-step workflows across enterprise systems. The company reports nearly 1,000 customers have already begun their agentic AI journey, with AI Agent Studio and Orchestrator becoming generally available in March 2025 .

ServiceNow CEO Bill McDermott forecasts that AI agents will save workers a day a week this year (a 20% productivity boost) and 2.5 days a week next year (a 50% boost), creating what he calls a “massive productivity dividend.” To support this vision, ServiceNow is acquiring conversational AI platform Cuein to enhance agents’ ability to analyze conversation data.

NVIDIA announced the Nemotron model families , including Llama Nemotron LLMs and Cosmos Nemotron VLMs, designed as foundation models for enterprise agentic AI. Built in collaboration with Meta, these models come in Nano, Super, and Ultra sizes and are optimized for tasks like instruction following, coding, and visual analysis. The models are available as NVIDIA NIM microservices for easy deployment.

Cohere launched North, an AI workspace platform optimized for air-gapped environments , positioning it as an enterprise-focused alternative to cloud-dependent agent platforms. The company partnered with Royal Bank of Canada as an early customer, reflecting financial services’ interest in AI solutions that can operate securely within regulated environments.

Developer Tools

JetBrains released Junie , an AI coding agent integrated directly into JetBrains IDEs. Junie achieves a 53.6% score on the SWE-Bench Verified benchmark, a measure of software engineering capability. The agent can handle code generation, debugging, and refactoring tasks within the development environment.

Postman added an AI agent builder combining LLMs with its API platform, allowing developers to create agents that can interact with APIs through natural language. This bridges the gap between API development and agentic AI, enabling agents to programmatically access services through Postman’s extensive API network.

Block (Jack Dorsey’s company) open-sourced Goose under the Apache 2.0 license, providing a framework for building AI agents that can be redirected mid-task—a critical capability for real-world applications where requirements change. The open-source approach contrasts with closed platforms and aims to accelerate experimentation.

Evaluation & Infrastructure

The ecosystem is maturing beyond basic agent creation. Galileo launched Agentic Evaluations , a platform for testing agent performance across multiple dimensions. Microsoft introduced pay-as-you-go access for AI agents with M365 Copilot Chat, addressing cost concerns by letting enterprises pay only for what they use.

Palo Alto Networks announced AI Runtime Security for protecting agents during execution, addressing growing security concerns as agents become more autonomous. NVIDIA released guardrails and tools specifically for enterprise agent deployment, including NeMo Guardrails and NIM microservices for safe production use.

Enterprise Reality Check: Enthusiasm Meets Integration Challenges

The enthusiasm for AI agents is real, but implementation is proving difficult. A comprehensive survey by eMarketer found that 93% of IT leaders are implementing or planning to implement AI agents within two years, but 80% cite data integration as a major obstacle. The average enterprise uses 897 apps, with only 29% interconnected, creating a fragmented data landscape that hinders agent effectiveness.

The UiPath 2025 Agentic AI Report, surveying 252 U.S. IT executives, reveals both optimism and practical barriers:

  • 90% have business processes that would be improved by agentic AI
  • 77% are prepared to invest in agentic AI this year
  • 56% identify IT security as a top concern
  • 35% cite integration with existing systems as a concern
  • 37% identify cost of implementation as a concern

A BCG survey of 1,803 executives found that one-third of companies plan to spend over $25 million on AI in 2025, reflecting significant investment commitment. However, the survey also identified a critical “ambition-results gap”: only 25% of executives report meaningful value from their AI initiatives. The survey found that leading companies focus AI investments on reshaping core functions (80% of investments) rather than just productivity gains (56% for other companies).

Real-world deployments are beginning to show concrete results:

  • Fujitsu achieved a 67% productivity boost by implementing Azure AI Agent Service to automate sales proposal creation, enabling around 38,000 employees to focus on customer engagement rather than document preparation
  • Baca Systems cut customer service response times from 5-7 minutes to 5-10 seconds using Salesforce agents, transforming the customer experience
  • Boost.ai and Sage deployed an accounting AI agent in just 50 days, demonstrating rapid implementation timelines
  • BNY has deployed 40 AI production use cases and made the platform available to all employees

Microsoft’s IT division, Microsoft Digital, is fundamentally restructuring around AI agents as “digital colleagues,” treating agents as core organizational components rather than optional tools. The company has also deployed employee-built agents for network infrastructure monitoring, demonstrating how organizations can extend AI platforms for internal operational tasks.

The gap between optimism and implementation remains the story. While surveys show strong enthusiasm, the complexity of enterprise data environments, security concerns, and the need for measurable ROI are slowing adoption. Research: Making Agents More Capable and Reliable

Agent reliability is improving through targeted research addressing core limitations in generalization, robustness, domain-specific reasoning, and security.

Researchers from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications developed AgentRefine, which uses a Dungeons & Dragons-inspired framework to teach AI agents self-correction. The approach improves agents’ ability to generalize and perform better on unfamiliar tasks and in new environments. Tested on models including GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama variants, AgentRefine enhanced adaptability and reduced errors, addressing a key limitation in current agent deployments.

MIT researchers discovered a counterintuitive finding they call the “indoor training effect”: training AI agents in noise-free environments actually leads to better performance in noisy conditions than training directly in noisy environments. The research, demonstrated using modified Atari games, challenges the conventional wisdom of matching training and testing environments. This finding could inform better training methods for AI agents deployed in uncertain real-world scenarios.

Pacific Northwest National Laboratory created CACTUS, an AI agent that connects LLM reasoning with cheminformatics tools for drug discovery. CACTUS can predict molecular properties, assess drug-likeness, and facilitate autonomous experimentation. The system runs on both consumer-grade hardware and supercomputers, democratizing access to computational chemistry tools and accelerating scientific research.

AMD and Johns Hopkins University built Agent Laboratory, a framework that automates scientific research processes including literature reviews, experimentation, and report writing. The system demonstrated an 84% reduction in research costs compared to existing autonomous methods while maintaining quality standards, with workflow costs dropping from $13.10 for o1-preview to $2.33 for gpt-4o.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) conducted agent hijacking evaluations using the AgentDojo framework. Working with the UK AI Security Institute, they found that optimized attacks could increase success rates from 11% to 81% on upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet. This research highlights the importance of continuous evaluation and improvement of security frameworks to mitigate hijacking risks, particularly for attacks like indirect prompt injection, remote code execution, and automated phishing.

These research advances address critical barriers to agent adoption: generalization beyond training data, robustness in uncertain conditions, domain-specific expertise, and security against hijacking. The focus is shifting from “can agents work?” to “how do we make agents reliable enough for production deployment?”

Funding: Vertical AI Agents Attract Major Capital

The funding landscape shows investors betting on vertical specialization over horizontal platforms. Healthcare AI attracted significant attention, with over $200M in funding during the period.

Hippocratic AI raised $141 million in Series B funding at a $1.64 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $278 million. The company launched a Healthcare AI Agent App Store with 300 AI agents covering 25 specialties. The safety network includes 6,000 nurses and 300 doctors providing oversight. Clinicians can create AI agent prototypes in 30 minutes and develop testable agents in 3-4 hours, with the company focusing on non-diagnostic clinical tasks to address healthcare staffing shortages.

Eleos secured $60 million in Series C funding for behavioral health AI agents, bringing total funding to over $120 million. The company provides an AI voice tool that runs in the background of therapy sessions to help clinicians analyze patient conversations, reducing administrative burden and improving documentation. Eleos expanded into 8 new states in 2024, now operating in 25 states total.

Auquan tripled revenue and closed an $8 million seed round for financial services AI agents. The company’s agents have helped top financial firms like MetLife and UBS eliminate over 50,000 hours of manual work, covering 550,000 entities and serving 25% of the top 25 private equity firms.

The pattern is clear: investors are betting on vertical applications that solve specific industry problems rather than general-purpose agent platforms. Healthcare stands out as the leading vertical, with clinical AI agents attracting significant capital to address staffing shortages while maintaining safety through clinician oversight networks.

Ecosystem Watch: From Agents to Infrastructure

The ecosystem is expanding beyond individual agents to infrastructure for multi-agent systems and specialized applications across industries.

Infrastructure Vision

Cisco’s Outshift group proposed an “Internet of Agents”, a new network infrastructure layer designed to enable AI agents from different organizations to automatically collaborate. The vision requires industry-wide cooperation to create open standards, security frameworks, and reference implementations for distributed agentic computing. Cisco published a research paper titled “DAWN: Designing Distributed Agents in a Worldwide Network” in November 2024, and the company’s research found that 78.1% of companies plan to develop and put their own AI agent into production, while 51.1% already have an agent in production.

PwC and Microsoft announced a strategic collaboration to bring AI agents to clients, combining PwC’s industry expertise with Microsoft’s agent platforms. The partnership aims to accelerate enterprise adoption by providing proven agent implementations across business functions.

Market Sentiment

The AI agent crypto sector experienced a sharp correction, losing 43.5% of its market value over a weekend—from a $20 billion peak to $11.3 billion. Major tokens like VIRTUAL, AI16Z, and FARTCOIN saw significant losses. Despite the downturn, analysts project potential long-term growth, with bull case estimates reaching up to $250 billion. The volatility highlights the speculative nature of crypto-based AI agent projects compared to enterprise-focused implementations.

Vertical Deployments

Specialized AI agents are entering production across diverse industries:

  • Element5 launched Neos for healthcare prior authorization, automating eligibility verifications and authorizations in post-acute care
  • Spot AI introduced the Remote Security Agent, described as the industry’s first remote Video AI Agent for physical security, addressing $94.5 billion in annual retail theft losses
  • Linq unveiled an AI agent for live events that automates lead capture from badges and business cards, reducing manual follow-up from days to minutes
  • Oracle announced AI agents for Fusion Cloud Sales that help sales teams automate administrative tasks, with Gartner predicting these technologies will reduce prospecting and meeting prep time by over 50% by 2026
  • SOCi reported that its Genius AI solutions now account for over 10% of its annual recurring revenue within eight months of launch, surpassing $100 million in ARR
  • Iterate AI uses Amazon MemoryDB to accelerate its workforce management conversational AI agent, demonstrating infrastructure optimization for agent performance

Dharmesh Shah’s Agent.xyz platform surpassed 250,000 users , reflecting growing end-user adoption. AI voice agents emerged as a key trend, with Andreessen Horowitz publishing a comprehensive update on the state of voice-based AI agents and their applications in customer service and sales.

Context-aware agents are becoming a focus area, with researchers and companies exploring agents that can understand and adapt to changing context during conversations—something Goose’s open-source framework specifically addresses by allowing mid-task redirection.

The infrastructure for multi-agent systems is being built. From Cisco’s Internet of Agents vision to specialized vertical applications, the ecosystem is moving beyond isolated agents to interconnected systems that can collaborate across organizational boundaries.

Looking Ahead: The Agentic Transition

January 2025 marked a transition point in the evolution of AI agents. OpenAI’s Operator launch validated agentic AI as the next major platform shift beyond chatbots. The platform announcements from ServiceNow, NVIDIA, Cohere, and others demonstrate this isn’t just research—it’s product.

Enterprise surveys reveal both enthusiasm and practical barriers. The 93% adoption figure from eMarketer and 77% investment readiness from UiPath show strong momentum, but the 80% citing data integration challenges and BCG’s finding that only 25% of executives report meaningful value underscore the implementation gap.

Real-world deployments are proving value with concrete metrics: Baca Systems’ response time reduction from 5-7 minutes to 5-10 seconds, Fujitsu’s 67% productivity boost, Boost.ai and Sage’s 50-day deployment. These aren’t demos—they’re production systems delivering measurable business results.

Research advances address core reliability issues. AgentRefine’s self-correction framework, MIT’s indoor training effect, CACTUS’s domain-specific reasoning, Agent Laboratory’s automated research processes, and NIST’s security evaluations all tackle the barriers between experimental agents and production-ready systems.

Funding concentrates on vertical applications, with healthcare attracting over $200M through Hippocratic AI and Eleos. Investors are betting that specialized agents solving specific industry problems will beat general-purpose platforms, at least in the near term.

The “Internet of Agents” vision from Cisco suggests where this could go: a network infrastructure layer enabling agents from different organizations to collaborate automatically. It’s an ambitious vision requiring industry-wide cooperation, but it acknowledges that the future of agentic AI isn’t just individual agents—it’s multi-agent systems working together.

Industry experts predict 2025 as the breakout year. OpenAI’s product chief Kevin Weil says humanity is on the verge of AI agents that can complete real-world tasks. Sam Altman predicts agents will enter the workforce in 2025. Gartner forecasts that by 2028, at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously by agentic AI, up from 0% in 2024.

The pieces are moving into place: models, platforms, evaluation tools, specialized applications, security infrastructure. The challenge now is execution at scale. The gap between demo and production remains, but the direction is clear: we’re moving from chatbots to agents, from tools to abilities.

As Vijoy Pandey, senior vice president at Cisco’s Outshift incubator, put it: “The rapid emergence of foundation model-based AI agents is driving us toward ensembles of multi-agent applications working together across the internet.” The verge is here.
